women in new towns were disadvantaged in a number of ways: in terms of their housing, employment opportunities and access to services.

women in the garden cities and new town movement were not able to achieve their aims because of the social context in which they operated and because of their own limitations in terms of social status, education and skills.

In summary, our research is concerned with
how the gendered nature of the new town movement has been reflected in its physical and social planning.
the extent to which women were enabled to participate in new town life and the reasons why they were not.
the extent to which the new towns were a 'demi-paradise' for women, and the extent to which women were able to shape them.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the new towns were a 'demi-paradise' for women, but not a paradise.
women were largely excluded from the new towns, and the gender division of labour was reinforced rather than challenged.
the new town movement was a male-dominated movement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
women's lives in garden cities and in new towns have been only 'demi-paradise'.
the new towns were not the only place where the gender order was reproduced, but they did provide a particularly powerful example of it, and of the way in which it was reproduced.
, in garden cities and in new towns, women have been largely absent from decision-making and that the physical environment of new towns has been shaped to meet male needs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the garden city and new towns movement, the vision of women as full citizens of new towns and garden cities has been largely forgotten.
the gendered nature of the planning process, and of planning practice in general, was a key element in the way in which new towns were planned, built and lived.
, despite Howard's vision, the garden city idea was not gender-neutral, and that it has had a significant impact on women's opportunities.
